questions.q: Under the Mitakshara school, a son's right to ancestral coparcenary property arises:
o: Only on the father's death
By BIRTH — an independent right that exists even during the father's lifetime
Only after marriage
Only if the father specifically grants it
questions.src: Mitakshara law is characterised by "unobstructed heritage" — the son acquires an interest in ancestral property by birth, distinct from Dayabhaga where the right arises only upon the owner's death.

questions.q: The Dayabhaga school of Hindu law is primarily followed in:
o: Most of India
West Bengal and Assam
Only Tamil Nadu
Only Maharashtra
questions.src: Dayabhaga is the school followed mainly in West Bengal and Assam, as distinguished from Mitakshara followed across most of the rest of India.

questions.q: In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that a daughter's coparcenary right under the amended Section 6:
o: Requires the father to be alive on 9 September 2005
Arises by birth and applies retrospectively, regardless of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005
Applies only to daughters born after 2005
Does not apply to Mitakshara families
questions.src: Vineeta Sharma resolved the conflicting earlier rulings — a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth, and this applies retrospectively; the father's survival on the amendment date is irrelevant.

questions.q: A Karta may validly alienate joint family property on which of the following grounds?
o: Personal preference alone, with no other justification needed
Legal Necessity, Benefit of the Estate, or Indispensable Duties
Only with unanimous written consent of every coparcener in every single instance
Karta can never alienate joint family property under any circumstances
questions.src: The three recognised grounds for valid alienation by a Karta are Legal Necessity, Benefit of the Estate, and Indispensable (religious/charitable) Duties.

questions.q: Under the Doctrine of Pious Obligation, a son is generally liable to pay off his father's debts EXCEPT where such debts are:
o: For business purposes
Avyavaharika — immoral or illegal in nature
Owed to a bank
Below a certain amount
questions.src: Sons are not liable under the pious obligation doctrine for their father's avyavaharika (immoral/illegal) debts.

questions.q: Under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, the minimum age for a valid marriage is:
o: 18 for both parties
Bridegroom 21, Bride 18
Bridegroom 18, Bride 21
25 for both parties
questions.src: Section 5 requires the bridegroom to have completed 21 years and the bride 18 years of age.

questions.q: In Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha, the Supreme Court held that a marriage without the customary ceremonies required under Section 7:
o: Is still valid if the couple genuinely intended to be married
Is NOT a valid marriage — mere intention to live as spouses is insufficient
Is valid only if registered
Depends solely on the length of cohabitation
questions.src: The Court held ceremonial compliance under Section 7 is mandatory; intention alone, without the required rites, does not create a valid Hindu marriage.

questions.q: A marriage where one party already has a living spouse at the time of the second marriage is:
o: Voidable at the innocent party's option
Void under Section 11
Valid if performed with proper ceremonies
Valid but only in certain states
questions.src: Section 11 declares such bigamous marriages void, since Section 5(i) mandates monogamy as a condition for a valid marriage.

questions.q: In Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chopra, the Supreme Court:
o: Struck down Section 9 (restitution of conjugal rights) as unconstitutional
Upheld the constitutional validity of Section 9, overturning the earlier T. Sareetha ruling
Abolished the remedy of judicial separation entirely
Held that restitution decrees can be physically enforced by the police
questions.src: The Supreme Court upheld Section 9's constitutionality, reversing the Andhra Pradesh High Court's earlier decision in T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah.

questions.q: Under Section 9, if a restitution of conjugal rights decree is not complied with (cohabitation not resumed) within a specified period, this becomes:
o: A criminal offence with imprisonment
A ground for divorce
Automatically void with no further consequence
Grounds for the respondent to claim damages
questions.src: Non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after a restitution decree becomes a ground for divorce under Section 13.

questions.q: A decree of Judicial Separation under Section 10, unlike divorce:
o: Permanently dissolves the marriage
Relieves parties of the obligation to cohabit WITHOUT dissolving the marriage itself
Requires both parties' consent in every case
Automatically converts to divorce after 6 months
questions.src: Judicial separation suspends cohabitation obligations without ending the marital status itself — distinct from divorce, which dissolves the marriage.

questions.q: Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act (maintenance pendente lite) is available to:
o: Only the wife, never the husband
Either spouse who lacks sufficient independent income, during the pendency of matrimonial proceedings
Only parties who have already obtained a divorce decree
Only parties married for more than 5 years
questions.src: Section 24 is a gender-neutral provision — either spouse lacking sufficient independent income can claim maintenance and litigation expenses during pending proceedings.

questions.q: Under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956, the paramount consideration in deciding a child's guardianship is:
o: Strictly following the statutory father-then-mother order with no exceptions
The welfare of the child, which can override the rigid statutory hierarchy
The wishes of the paternal grandparents
The income level of each parent alone
questions.src: Courts have consistently emphasised the welfare of the child as the paramount consideration, capable of overriding the bare statutory guardianship order, especially for children of tender years.

questions.q: Under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, Class I heirs of a deceased Hindu male (including son, daughter, widow, mother) inherit:
o: In strict order, one category at a time
Simultaneously — all Class I heirs share together, to the exclusion of Class II heirs and beyond
Only sons inherit; daughters are excluded
Only if there is a valid will
questions.src: Class I heirs under Section 8 inherit simultaneously, taking priority over Class II heirs, agnates, and cognates.

questions.q: Under Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act, property a Hindu FEMALE inherited from her PARENTS, in the absence of her children, generally devolves upon:
o: Her husband's heirs automatically
Her parents' heirs — reverting to her natal family in this specific circumstance
The state, since it cannot be inherited further
Whichever relative applies first to court
questions.src: Section 15's special devolution rule sends property inherited from parents back to the parents' heirs (not the husband's side) when there are no surviving children — a distinct rule protecting the natal family's interest.

questions.q: The 2005 Amendment to the Hindu Succession Act primarily achieved which major reform?
o: Abolished all forms of coparcenary entirely
Conferred coparcenary rights on daughters by birth, on par with sons
Removed maintenance rights from Hindu wives
Made all Hindu marriages compulsorily registered
questions.src: The 2005 Amendment substituted Section 6 to give daughters coparcenary rights by birth, equal to sons, in Mitakshara coparcenary property.

questions.q: "Notional Partition" (relevant under the pre-2005 Section 6 proviso) refers to:
o: An actual, physical division of joint family property carried out by a court
A legal fiction deeming a partition to have occurred immediately before a coparcener's death, solely to calculate that person's share for succession purposes
A partition that only daughters could demand
A partition that requires no legal basis at all
questions.src: Notional partition is a legal fiction used purely for calculating a deceased coparcener's share for succession purposes, not an actual physical division.

questions.q: A "Coparcenary" under Hindu law is best described as:
o: Identical in scope to the broader Hindu Joint Family
A narrower body within the joint family, consisting of those who acquire an interest in ancestral property by birth and can demand partition
A term with no fixed legal meaning
Applicable only to female members
questions.src: Coparcenary is narrower than the joint family — it specifically refers to those members (traditionally sons, now including daughters post-2005) who acquire a birthright and can enforce partition.

questions.q: Under Hindu law, a wife is generally entitled to live separately from her husband and still claim maintenance where there is:
o: No circumstance justifies this — she must always live with her husband to claim maintenance
Cruelty, desertion, husband having another wife living, conversion, or other justifying cause
Only if she has independent wealth
Only after a formal divorce decree
questions.src: The Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act 1956 recognises specified circumstances (cruelty, desertion, bigamy, conversion, other justifying cause) where a wife may live separately without forfeiting her maintenance rights.

questions.q: Under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act 1956, a valid adoption generally requires:
o: No conditions at all — any adoption is automatically valid
Capacity of the adopter, capacity of the person giving in adoption, and the adoptee being capable of being taken in adoption per statutory conditions
Only the consent of the child being adopted
Court approval in every single case regardless of other conditions
questions.src: Valid adoption under the 1956 Act requires satisfying conditions relating to the adopter's capacity, the giver's capacity, and the adoptee's eligibility under the Act.

questions.q: "Sapinda relationship" as a bar to marriage under Section 5 refers to:
o: Any two people of the same religion
A degree of blood/marriage relationship within which marriage is prohibited unless custom permits
Only relationships by adoption
A term with no relevance to Hindu marriage law
questions.src: Sapinda relationships fall within a prohibited degree for marriage under Section 5, unless a custom or usage governing the parties permits such a marriage.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ground for a VOIDABLE (not void) Hindu marriage under Section 12?
o: Bigamy — a spouse already living at the time of marriage
Marriage within a prohibited degree
Consent obtained by fraud or force, or the respondent being pregnant by someone other than the petitioner at the time of marriage
The parties belonging to different castes
questions.src: Section 12 lists voidable grounds including impotency, fraud/force in obtaining consent, and pre-marriage pregnancy by another person — distinct from Section 11's void grounds (bigamy, prohibited degree, sapinda).

questions.q: The Family Courts Act 1984 was enacted primarily to:
o: Abolish all matrimonial remedies under personal laws
Establish specialised courts to encourage conciliation and settlement in family disputes before contested litigation
Replace the Hindu Marriage Act entirely
Handle only criminal matters involving families
questions.src: Family Courts were established to provide a specialised forum emphasising conciliation and amicable settlement of family disputes, alongside adjudication when settlement fails.

questions.q: Under Hindu law, "unobstructed heritage" (as under Mitakshara) refers to property in which the right:
o: Arises only after the current owner's death
Arises by BIRTH, independent of the current holder's death
Never passes to any heir
Can only be claimed by adopted children
questions.src: Unobstructed heritage (Mitakshara characteristic) means the right vests by birth, not obstructed by needing the current holder to first pass away — contrasted with "obstructed heritage" (Dayabhaga), where the right arises only on death.

questions.q: Under the Hindu Marriage Act, "irretrievable breakdown of marriage" as an independent statutory ground for divorce:
o: Is explicitly and directly listed as a ground under Section 13
Is not an explicit statutory ground under Section 13, though courts have sometimes invoked it via Article 142 powers in exceptional Supreme Court cases
Was abolished by the 2005 Amendment
Applies only to marriages solemnised after 2005
questions.src: Irretrievable breakdown is NOT an explicit statutory ground under Section 13 — it has occasionally been invoked by the Supreme Court using its special Article 142 constitutional powers in exceptional cases, but Parliament has not made it a general statutory ground for ordinary courts.
